en: Having prostrated with mind, speech, and body before the Omniscient One who is the Friend of All,
this *Kāvyālaṃkāra* shall be composed according to my understanding.
It produces proficiency in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as in the arts; it brings joy and fame through the composition of excellent poetry. (Bh 1.2)

Like the generosity of one who is destitute, like the skill with weapons of a eunuch, like the eloquence of an ignorant man, and like the knowledge of the scriptures of one who is not a poet. (Bh 1.3)
Without discipline, what is glory? Without the moon, what is night? And devoid of true poetry, what kind of eloquence can there be? (Bh 1.4)
Even those of dull intellect are capable of studying the scriptures through the instruction of a guru;
however, poetry arises only occasionally in someone possessed of creative intuition (pratibhā).
Even for those who have gone to heaven and composed excellent literary works,
their beautiful body consisting of poetry remains indeed free from decay.
As long as his imperishable fame fills the two worlds,
so long indeed does that virtuous man dwell in the realm of the gods.
Therefore, one who desires a fame that endures for as long as the earth lasts,
and who has understood what is to be known, must apply effort toward the characteristics of poetry.
Grammar, prosody, lexicography, the Itihāsas, narratives based on them,
the world, logic, and the arts— these should be considered the causes of poetry.
The causes of poetry; [Udbhaṭa’s commentary (see GNOLI 1962, p. XL);
"kāvyagairhyamī" / edM;
"kāvyayairvaśī"].
Having understood that these [objects] are denoted by words through poetic means, and having performed the service of those who know them— [that is,] the service of those who know them—
[one attains the goal].
Having observed that [work], its worship by the learned, and other treatises, one should apply oneself with devotion to the composition of poetry. (Bh 1.10)
In every respect, not even a single faulty word should be uttered;
for one is censured by poetry that lacks proper characteristics, just as one is by a bad son.
Lack of poetic skill leads neither to unrighteousness, nor to disease, nor to punishment.
Furthermore, the wise declare that bad poetry is death personified.
Ornaments such as metaphor and the like have been described by others in many ways;
for even the face of a beautiful woman does not shine if it is devoid of adornment. (Bh 1.13)
Others declare that external ornament consists of figures such as *rūpaka*;
they desire the grammatical derivation of nouns (*sup*) and verbs (*tiṅ*) to be the ornament of speech. (Bh 1.14)
Regarding this, they say: "This is merely linguistic elegance; such is not the thorough understanding of meaning.
Rather, we accept both: the distinction between verbal ornaments and the ornaments of the expressed meaning. (Bh 1.15)
Word and meaning together constitute poetry; it is of two kinds: prose and verse. It is also threefold: Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and other Apabhraṃśa. (Bh_1.16)

Furthermore, it is divided into four types: that which recounts the deeds of gods and others who have already lived, that which has an invented plot, and that which is based on the arts and sciences. Bh_1.17.

The epic composition (sargabandha), the dramatic work for performance (abhineyārtha), as well as the narrative (ākhyāyikā) and the tale (kathā), and the unstructured poetry (anibaddha)— that [poetry] is further said to be of five kinds.
A Mahākāvya is a composition consisting of cantos, which is great both because it concerns great persons and because it is itself grand;
it employs non-vulgar words, possesses meaningful content, is adorned with poetic figures, and rests upon an excellent foundation.

That [work], which possesses the fivefold junctures— consisting of counsel, envoys, expeditions, battle, and the triumph of the leader— is endowed with prosperity and should not be over-explained. (1.20)
This theme need not be explained further—it will famously recur below at 2.20:

"Even though it sets forth the four aims of human life, it provides instruction on many other matters; it is consistent with the nature of the world and possesses all the aesthetic sentiments individually. (Bh 1.21)
Having first introduced the hero by means of his lineage, prowess, learning, and so forth,
one should not describe his own death with the intention of exalting another.
If that [excellence] is not intended to pervade the body of poetry, then the mention of "mudhā" (in vain) and so forth in the praise of one who possesses prosperity would be pointless. Bh_1.23.
The *grahaṇa* and the *stava*:
whatever [is composed in] *nāṭaka*, *dvipadī*, *śamyā*, *rāsaka*, *skandhaka*, and so forth.
That has been stated for the purpose of dramatic representation; its detailed exposition has been given by others.
[He spoke] with words whose sounds, meanings, and syntactical structures were refined, unconfused, and pleasant to hear,
[which were] refined (*saṃskṛta*), natural (*prakṛta*),
and flowing (*prasṛta*).
That which is composed in prose, possesses exalted meaning, and is divided into sections called *ucchvāsa*s, is considered an *ākhyāyikā*. (Bh 1.25)
In that [form], the conduct of the hero’s own deeds is narrated, as well as the *vakra* and *aparavakra* meters, which at the appropriate time indicate future events. (Bh 1.26)
It is marked by certain narratives composed according to the author's intention.
It is filled with the abduction of maidens, battles, and the arising of separations.
It is not composed in the Vaktra or Aparavaktra meters, nor does it contain the Ucchvāsa sections;
its activity is both refined and unrefined, and it likewise partakes of the vernacular Apabhraṃśa.
The conditioned and the unconditioned;
by others her own conduct is described therein, but it is not spoken of by the Leader.
How could a person of noble birth manifest his own virtues?
How is it that people [say]: "In whatever way" (kathaṃcana);
furthermore, that which is unbound, such as a mere verse or a śloka, and so forth.
It is appropriate that all this is accepted through the expression of a crooked nature.
Other wise men maintain that there is another [style], the Vaidarbha; and they hold that this alone is superior, while the other, even if it possesses good meaning, is not. (Bh 1.31)
"Is this Gaudīya and that Vaidarbha style different?
For those of dull intellect, they are merely distinguished by various names according to the logic of following what has gone before. (Bh. 1.32)
But is it not the case that [the style] beginning with the Āśmaka lineage is called Vaidarbha?
Granted, let it be so; for generally, designation is established according to one's desire.
This [work], however, has undeveloped meaning, lacks eloquent expression, and though clear, straightforward, and gentle, it is disjointed like a song that is merely pleasant to the ear. (Bh 1.34)
That which is free from vulgarity like an ornament, purposeful, logical, and unconfused—
whether it be the Gauḍīya style, it is superior, and not otherwise, as is the Vaidarbha.
Beauty of speech does not arise merely from extreme [length] and so forth;
rather, the ornament of words is held to be the expression of meanings and sounds through indirect or figurative turns of phrase. (Bh 1.36)

[The six faults of poetry: Poets do not employ that which is of interpretable meaning, that which is obscure, that which has a different meaning, that which is non-expressive, that which is illogical, or that which contains words with hidden meanings. (Bh_1.37)

That whose meaning is led by the wise through force to a definitive sense—though it does not conform to the logic of words—is [the *neyārtha*], being interpreted only by some internal intention. (Bh 1.38)
Just as the notion that "Bhadrā is like an illusion" is an improper conceptualization,
so too do they lead [the world] by means of words such as "Veṇudāki," even in the absence of [actual] speech.
They lead her away (tāṃ nayanti); they lead them away (tān niyanti). Several interpretations of this example are presented in [the commentary].
One should know that which is afflicted and obstructed as having another meaning,
just as [the word] "vigama" [is used] in the sense of "departure."
When their purpose had vanished, those women dwelt in his grief and in that distorted state of play.
The *anyārtha* (meaning something else) is "effected by the *vi*" [in *vijahruḥ*]. This would apparently fall under the category of *avācaka* (non-expressive) for Mammaṭa: "BHĀMaha 1.41:

*himāpahāmitradharair vyāptam vyomety avācakam / sākṣād arūḍham vācyerthe nābhidhānam pratīyate //* [The phrase] "the sky is pervaded by those who bear the enemy of the fire that destroys cold" is non-expressive (*avācaka*), because the denotation is not perceived as being directly established in the expressed meaning."
This would apparently fall under the category of *kliṣṭa* (defective) for Mammaṭa;
for example: "The messengers are clouds, winds, and moons.
[Note: *mārutendavaḥ* is the reading.]
Likewise,
bees, hārītas, ruddy geese, parrots, and others [are included] among those [who possess the same qualities]. (1.42)
Likewise, there are bees, *edam*, and *edb*; therein are the *abhramara* and *hārīta* [birds], those who are speechless and those with indistinct speech, wandering through distant lands.
It is not logical by any reasoning that they should resort to the role of messengers. (Bh 1.43)
And if, out of longing, one speaks thus like a madman, let it be so; for this is frequently employed even by those of great intelligence. (Bh 1.44)
And the use of obscure terminology should not be employed under any circumstances; for this does not even conduce to the benefit of those who are wise. (Bh 1.45)
May the Lord of the dwellers of heaven, whose gaze is like that of a serpent, whose teeth are white,
and who is seen with pure vision, utterly destroy your enemies with his unerring arrows.
May the Lord of the earth, who dwells upon the mountain that devours the darkness of night, whose sight is unerring, and who gazes with bright eyes,
strike down your enemies with these showers of light.
With the assistance of Ratneśvarasūri’s commentary on the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*:
"There are four other defects:
those corrupted by sound (*śrutiduṣṭa*), those corrupted by meaning (*arthaduṣṭa*), and also those corrupted by construction (*kalpanāduṣṭa*)."
Likewise, they say that speech has four kinds of defects, including harshness to the ear.
The manifestations of excrement, feces, putrid matter, moist matter, severed matter,
vomited matter,
and flowing matter.
They are constrained by the heart’s expulsion of the upward-moving breaths that have been suppressed by their outward movement.
Their hearts were constrained; [the reading] *hṛdayantṛtāḥ* appears in edBGa.
Hiraṇyaretas (Agni) was crowded together, and the birds standing nearby were delicate.
And those utterances characterized by harshness of speech and so forth are considered "defective in hearing" (śrutiduṣṭa).

Furthermore, that which is corrupted in meaning (arthaduṣṭa) should be known as that where, upon being uttered, an understanding arises whose object is an indecent thing, by means of words expressive of such things; for example: [the verse beginning with] "mṛṇālavalayādi...".
For one who is intent on killing, who is arrogant, and who seeks out a vulnerability.
A fall inevitably occurs, and rising again is achieved only with great difficulty.
Whatever undesirable consequence arises from the conjunction of these two words,
it manifests itself.
Then they say: "That which is marred by conceptual construction is like one who wears the ornaments of bravery [without the reality of valor]. (1.52)
They know that such [usage] as "ajihladat" and so forth is harsh for the ear;
the skillful do not desire it, while others indeed consider it to be like a boil. (Bh 1.53)
However, due to a particular arrangement, even that which is poorly spoken shines, like a blue *palāśa* flower strung among other flowers in a garland. (Bh 1.54)
Even that which is improper may assume beauty through the excellence of its basis,
like dark collyrium applied to the eyes of a beloved.

O lotus-eyed one, this face of yours with its pale cheeks has truly lived up to the meaning of the word *gaṇḍa*, as it was well-said [by the etymologists]: "It is from association with the word *pāṇḍu* that it is called *gaṇḍa*. (Bh 1.56)
By this same principle, other improper things that are logically consistent should also be understood;
for example, [the case of] elephants whose temples are overflowing with rut-fluids.
Just as four hundred elephants with temples moistened by rut might employ [a task],
so too should one employ that which is more effective and that which is less effective. (1.58)

"This flower is fragrant and should be taken; this one is rustic and should be set aside. Thus does a garland-maker, having understood well, arrange them so that the composition gains beauty. In the same way, a word should be employed in poetic compositions by one whose mind is attentive. (Bh 1.59)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Bhāmahālaṅkāra*.
The second chapter:
Those of keen intellect, desiring sweetness and clarity, do not employ too many compound words. (Bh 2.1)
Some, wishing to express vigor, compose even many [verses] together, such as:
"Her locks are tawny with the pollen of mandāraka flowers. (Bh 2.2)
Poetry is desired to be sweet, pleasant to hear, not overly full of compound words, clear in its meaning so as to be understood by scholars, women, and children alike, and possessed of lucidity.
Alliteration, Yamaka, Metaphor, Illuminator, and Simile—these five alone are declared by others to be the ornaments of speech. (Bh 2.4)
They declare that alliteration (*anuprāsa*) consists in the arrangement of similar forms and sounds; O beloved, what is the use of such excessive concern regarding this, as has been stated? (Bh 2.5)
But other wise men consider another type to be vulgar alliteration; for example:
"Bala, whose throat was crowded with swarms of blue bees clinging to his garlands. (Bh 2.6)
Speech that possesses manifold meanings, is melodious, and does not consist of discordant syllables— by means of this middle path of reasoning, such beautiful words are produced.
Others also desire alliteration in the Lāṭīya style, as for example:
"Cast your gaze, which is a pleasure to behold, upon the moon risen from the moon-like face. (Bh 2.8)
The yamaka at the beginning, middle, and end; the repetition of a foot; likewise the "garland" (avalī); and the yamaka of all feet—this is said to be fivefold.
The inclusion of the *sandaṣṭaka*, *samudga*, and so forth is considered to be within this very category;
they may occur at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. Thus, there are exactly five types, as follows.
By that virtuous one, through his own virtue, royal power was maintained;
he acted in harmony with those who were harmonious, bringing people together with those who were united.
The virtuous person, fearing this essence-less cycle of existence, brings an end to the afflictions and proceeds upon the path of peace.
Desiring the cessation of births, diseases, and the power of those things difficult to subdue, cut off your attachment to the lower and adopt the method of liberation.
Of those difficult to tame: edM;
of those following wrong methods:
edB; of those lacking compassion: edBGa.
Desiring superiority, cut off [the pride of] being free from crookedness;
desiring excellence,
cut off [the pride of] being made of pearl.
O wise one, you are not attached to these delightful pleasures;
for even sages, when attached to those things which are delightful, are carried away by them.
With feet repeatedly placed upon one another, she has dark and light eyes, beautiful breasts and lips, and is full of joy; her intoxication is manifest, and she wears a garland of choice jewels.
With thick, dark, and dense tresses, this beloved woman both excites longing and brings it to its end.

These kings, who have granted complete charters and whose commands are never obstructed; who punish those who commit offenses and those who deviate from the path; and who occupy such thrones according to the succession of their ancestors.
In this same way, [the yamaka] may occur at the end of the first and third feet, or the second and fourth;
and when it occurs throughout all four feet, such a complete *samastapādayamaka* is difficult to compose well.
It is difficult [to distinguish] between words that have identical phonetic forms but differ in their referents from one another.
Furthermore, that which is a repetition of syllables is called a *yamaka*.

The *yamaka* (rhyme) favored by the learned is considered to consist of words that are well-known, full of vigor, with closely joined word-sandhis, clear, and possessing its own distinct expression. (Bh 2.18)
That which possesses a profound meaning through various elements and is expressed with double meanings is indeed called a *prahelikā* (enigma), as stated by Rāmaśarman in the *Acyutottara*.
If even these poetic works must be understood through commentary like technical treatises, then alas, they are a festival for the wise alone; the dull-witted, however, are ruined.
When the true nature of the object of comparison is described by means of a standard of comparison,
having perceived the equality of their qualities, the wise know that as *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).
Metaphor (rūpaka) is declared to be of two kinds: that which has all things as its object and that which manifests in part; this is explained as follows.
The lofty clouds, like elephants, are intoxicated by the spray of water;
emerging forth, these elephants of Indra’s bow are in a state of rut.
These [clouds],
gladdening [the world], are the ornaments of the forest of Indra’s bow;
they cause Indra’s rainbow to rejoice.
Of those whose girth-bands are wreaths of lightning and who bear the offerings of cranes.
The deep roar of the rain-clouds torments that beloved of mine.
The lamp is held to be threefold according to its objects—beginning, middle, and end;
because that single [lamp] exists in three states, it is thus divided into three kinds. (Bh 2.25)
These [three] make its name meaningful by illuminating its sense;
and this is demonstrated in three ways through three illustrations, as follows. (Bh 2.26)
Intoxication produces pleasure, which brings about love that is fragile with pride.
He [experienced] the longing for union with his beloved and the unbearable grief of his mind.
Spring adorns the women who wear garlands and fine garments,
and it adorns the foothills of the mountains with the songs of green pigeons and parrots.
The summer heat desires to bring an end to the forest groves, to rivers whose waters are drying up,
to the hearts of travelers, and to the very lives of living beings. (2.29)

When there is a similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison through even a slight quality— despite their being opposed in terms of place, time, action, and so forth— that is the figure of speech known as *upamā*.
The words *yathā* and *eva* express similarity between two things that possess distinct qualities, as in:
"She is dark like a blade of durva grass; she is slender like the śyāmā creeper. (Bh 2.31)
śyāmaṃ /edM/edB; śyāmā /edBGha % śyāmālatā /edM/ edB; śyāmalatā /edBGa/edBGha
Without the words *yathā* and *iva*, the comparison is expressed through a compound, as in "lotus-petal-eyed" (*kamalapatrākṣī*) and "moon-faced" (*śaśāṅkavadanā*). (Bh 2.32)
Even by one who possesses [the suffix] *vat*, a similarity of action is expressed in exactly that same way:
"He studies like a twice-born" (*dvijātivad adhīte*) or "He instructs us like a teacher" (*guruvad anuśāsti naḥ*). (Bh 2.33)

The *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence) is defined by the presentation of parallel subjects, because even when words such as "just as" (*yathā*) or "even so" (*iva*) are not explicitly stated, the equality of qualities is nevertheless perceived. (Bh 2.34)
In this case, a quality such as being common to both the virtuous and others is distinguished;
it brings about equality between those two, even when they are in opposition.
How many virtuous people are there who share their prosperity with the good?
Or how many are the roadside trees that bend under the weight of fruits sweet in both flavor and ripeness?
As for that which was stated by certain great beings regarding its threefold nature, it is here explained as being due to the distinctions of censure, praise, and the desire to communicate. (Bh 2.37)
Since the general qualities have already been indicated, has not all three [types of comparison] already been mentioned?
Indeed, every further elaboration, such as the "garland simile" (mālopamā) and so forth, is merely a useless prolixity.
The occurrence of inferiority, difference in gender or number, reversal, excessiveness of the standard of comparison, and dissimilarity—these are [faults]. (Bh 2.39)
These seven defects of similes have been set forth by the wise;
here they are described individually, along with their illustrations and defining characteristics.
With his yellow garment stirred by the wind, gracefully bearing a lotus that shone like the moon,
the hero of the Yadus, holding his Śārṅga bow, shone like a cloud accompanied by Indra’s rainbow.
As cited by Namisādhu in his commentary on Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 11:24:
"Here, indeed, the bow is shown by the seizing of the rainbow [which is] moon-shining conch-shell" (with *śaśibhāsi śaṅkham* as a lectio facilior?).
Because it lacks clothing and a conch shell, it is called "deficient. (Bh 2.42)
There is no entity whatsoever that possesses complete similarity with everything else;
rather, comparisons are employed by the learned according to what is appropriate for the purpose at hand.
Where is the moon with its unbroken orb, and where is the face of a beloved woman with its present luster?
It is merely because of some slight commonality of radiance that she is compared to the moon.
Furthermore, the poetry of great souls need not be interpreted according to technical definitions;
for is it not observed that total conformity [to rules] is as described by Rājamitra?

When the eyes of the lotuses had closed at the rays of the sun, and they were rendered motionless by the wind, the cries of the peacocks ceased within their mouths— like virtuous wives bereft of their husbands remaining in their own homes.
*vineśuḥ* /edM/edB;
*vineduḥ* /edBKa. This verse is cited by Vāmana in his *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* on 4.2.10.
From his mouth, as it were, there issued forth blazing arrows situated within the circle of his bow;
they appeared like streams of water flaming as they issue from the sun at midday when it is surrounded by a halo.
The cultivation of vegetables [an illustration of the impossible (*asambhava*);
quoted in the tenth chapter (*ullāsa*) of Mammaṭa’s *Kāvyaprakāśa*].
How could there be a morning downpour of rays from the blazing sun?
Because this is impossible according to reason, it is therefore called "impossible. (Bh 2.48)
In that case, what wise person would employ a comparison with something impossible?
Who indeed would make a comparison of the hare-marked moon with fire? (Bh 2.49)
How can that which possesses an extraordinary object be considered impossible?
For the state of possessing an extraordinary object is desired in the case of similes and poetic conceits (utprekṣā), as is well known. (Bh 2.50)
This elephant shines like a mass of darkness gathered together,
like a lake with water clear from autumn, or like a fragment of the sky left behind.
Note that, for Bhāmaha,
*liṅgabheda* (discrepancy of gender) is not a defect in comparisons (*upamā*) when the genders are masculine and neuter,
as he explains below (2:57).
Now, the distinction of gender and number is stated along with its exceptions;
that [distinction] is twofold due to deficiency or excess, and all three are explained as follows.
You are unfordable even for women whose minds are fixed on no other,
like a river whose waves are shattered upon jagged rocks for one who wishes to cross it.
Like a dog that advances at one point and strikes down at another by pouncing,
you have shattered the army of your enemies like a herd of deer.
In his commentary on *edM*, [the editor] notes that this verse is cited in Keśavamiśra’s *Alaṅkāraśekhara* (V.1):
"This ruddy sheldrake, seated upon a lotus, shines resplendent like the Lord Brahmā at the beginning of an eon, desiring to create all living beings. (Bh_2.55)
Indeed, the hand is compared to a blooming lotus,
and the lower lip to a piece of coral and to the bimba fruit in its luster.
It is said: "Granted that this exists; however, this rule applies only to women and men, and it is not accepted by others even for all three genders."
Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa assumed a form both charming and formidable,
like a cloud at night charged with lightning and the bow of Indra, joined by the moon.

This superiority [of Rāmaśarman] over Śaśin (the moon) is indeed due to his being seized by Rāma; for here, the lotus—which would otherwise be expressed as the object of comparison—is not actually mentioned. Bh_2.59 //
*jalaja* [edM]; *jalada* [edB]. Here, *jalaja* must refer to the conch.
The rule that "there is no complete similarity" has been explained in detail.
One should not, according to the poet's intention, apply the term "lotus" (jalaja) here [to the eyes].
Bhāmaha may intend to suggest that he is not dogmatic on this point by implying that Rāmaśarman might have intended the disproportion.
"An excess of the objects of comparison is proper; there should be no deficiency.
[The reading *nyāyyaṃ* is supported by edM and edB.]
It is right that the fame of cows, milk, the kunda flower, and the ploughshare should be equal in their purity. (2.61)
Surely similarity is expressed by means of a single comparison alone;
for the employment of what has already been stated does not sustain the weight of the meaning.
No answer was given to this objection.
Then, in that forest, there were elephants following their mates, their temples moistened by flowing rut.
(Quoted by Namisādhu ad Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 11:24)
The elephants, sporting with their mates and with temples wet from flowing rut,
and the peacocks adorned with variegated plumage, shone like planets of pure form in the sky.
Even if it is argued that there is a resemblance between elephants and the like and the planets, nevertheless, they possess either a brilliance or a ferocity similar to those [planets].
Thus have the varieties of simile been described, and another will be stated hereafter;
furthermore, a distinction different from [simile and other] ornaments is now being declared.

[Six other ornaments: Paraleipsis (ākṣepa), Corroboration by another matter (arthāntaranyāsa), Contrast (vyatireka), Poetic Concealment (vibhāvanā), Elliptical Exaggeration (samāsokti), and Hyperbole (atiśayokti) are the six further ornaments. Bh_2.66 //
In that regard, the objection concerning the subject matter both yet to be stated and already stated is considered to be of two kinds;
the remaining ones will be pointed out in their proper order as being of a single form.
The wise describe *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) as that which is like a negation of something intended, for the purpose of wishing to express a specific distinction; they say it is of two kinds, as follows.
[Regarding the term] *ākṣepa*:
"If I were not to see you even for a single moment, I would then be full of longing."
Let this much suffice for you; what is the use of saying anything else that is unpleasant to you?
"Let there be only this much, and nothing else"—
[this is an objection regarding the subject matter to be explained].
It is a marvel that you, who have traversed the earth with your own prowess, possess no arrogance.
Or what cause is sufficient for bringing about a transformation in the ocean? (2.70)
What indeed is the sufficient reason, or what is the sufficient bridge,
for the presentation of another matter apart from that which has already been stated?
That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by another matter) when it follows upon the preceding subject, as for example: [Bh 2.71].
You feel no distress when about to enter formidable enemy armies;
for whether good or bad, it is one's own self that reveals the future of men.
Because the meaning of "cause" is also expressed by the word *hi*,
this *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) is manifested all the more clearly for the sake of establishing what has been stated, as follows: [Bh_2.73]
The mountains carry even heavy clouds that have approached them; for one who is truly great indeed bears those who are great when they come to him out of affection.

When there is an object possessing a point of comparison, that which demonstrates its specific distinction is intended as "vyatireka" (dissimilarity), because it brings about a particularization, as for example: [Bh 2.75]
Your eyes, with their rows of lashes, are white and black, bordered by a coppery hue;
they are like a white lotus and a blue lotus, respectively, being one-sidedly pure white and dark blue.

When an action is prohibited, the manifestation of its result is to be known as "manifestation" (vibhāvanā) itself, even though the means for achieving it would otherwise be easily available. (Bh 2.77)
The peacocks have not yet drunk [the rain], the quarters of the sky are restless with longing,
the *nīpa* tree is fragrant though unanointed, and the water remains turbid, unstirred by falling drops.
